rows.evidence: Q1: Chapter 4 (Fig. 34, Fig. 45) reports the authors' own model runs of network cost under 10-100 randomly generated flow regimes with 50 repetitions; Chapter 5 Applications 1-4 report own AKLA/indexed-curve runs on Italian networks (Lecce, Sinistra Ofanto); Annex 1 reports own 1991 field discharge recordings at district 4 used to calibrate the Cl<U+00E9>ment r coefficient (Tables A3, A4).
rows.notes: The document is an FAO design/analysis manual (I&D Paper 59) with embedded original applications, so Q1 is answered yes with some doubt. It does not report any result comparing the investment cost of on-demand networks with that of other delivery schedules, nor any measured cost premium attributable to guaranteeing peak-period supply. What it shows: on-demand pipe diameters are computed for a probabilistic peak discharge (Cl<U+00E9>ment formulas, 'elasticity of the network' eR>1 in Fig. 10), the optimal network cost rises and then stabilises as more flow regimes are included (Fig. 34, Fig. 45, cost of example network ~190-215 million ITL), and performance/reliability of existing on-demand networks under peak demand (Figs. 57, 69-77). Chapter 6 lists management conditions (holding size, volumetric pricing, energy cost) as general experience, not own findings on investment cost. The claimed effect (higher investment cost of on-demand networks) is at most implied by design logic, not established by the study's own result.

notes: Full text appears complete (chapters 1-6, Annexes 1-3). The publication combines a methods manual, software description (COPAM), and original applications; only the original applications and Annex 1 calibration were treated as the study's own results.
